## Reproducible Data Science

### The Importance of Reproducible Research: Main Steps

You should always show, how you got to the results of your research, so other people can check your research and reproduce it. They could potentially also
create new experiments based on your work, which means they need to be able to understand your reasoning and the steps you took to get to your results. 
The UZH has a center for [Reproducable Science](!https://www.crs.uzh.ch/en.html) that provides help and instructions on how to conduct reproducable science and research.


### Open Science and FAIR Data Principles

**Open Science** is a term that describes the practice of making all types of scientific resources (data, results, methods, etc.) publicly available at every stage of the research process. Open Science aims to improve the efficiency and quality of research, and has many advantages in various fields.
The main key areas of Open Science are:
- Public access to scientific data and services, including codes, publications, and sources;
- Publications are registered as open (Open Access) when they are digital, online, free of charge, and free of copyright and licensing restrictions.
- Research methods that are reproducible, replicable, transparent, efficient, and improve the robustness of scientific services
- The implementation of cultural change within university structures and the working methods of researchers.
[The University of Zurich] (https://www.openscience.uzh.ch/de/open-science-an-uzh.html) engages with Open Science at an international and national level and is part of various initiatives.

The **FAIR data principles** are a fundamental part of open science, which implies the following:
- **Findable**: data must be easily findable and machine-readable, and have a unique persistent identifier.
- **Accessible**: data and publications must be accessible to everyone.
- **Interoperable**: data must be processed using open-source software that is easily downloadable and usable.
- **Re-usable**: everything must be documented for future studies to be re-used.
It is necessary that the data used in research follow the FAIR data principles so that the research is as accessible and reproducible as possible.

Main steps to make your work reproducible: 
- Provide tested and documented source code
- Use dependencies that are easy to find and install
- Use open-source programming languages
- Use open-source operating systems
- Make raw data and data scripts accessible to everyone
- Preregister your research

### Colour Palettes

Explain how to use colour palettes effectively, which types of palettes are best suited to different kinds of data, and what factors should be considered when selecting an appropriate colour scheme.

It is important to choose appropriate colours to represent you data. The chosen palette should reflect the meaning of the variable. Colours make the figures more appealing and memorable. In papers/reports, you have to prioritize consistency and readability.

Types of palettes:
Sequential palettes: for ordered data or magnitude/intensity/frequency (Exp.: population density)
Diverging scales: data with meaningful midpoint or direction & magnitude of difference (Exp.: correlation from -1 to 1)
Categorical/qualitative palettes: for unordered/categorical data; no implied ordering (Exp.: countries)

It is important to consider accessibility when choosing colour palettes. For example, colour blind people won't perceive the colours the same way as someone who isn't colour blind. It is also important to check the contrast between light and dark backgrounds and text. Also, the number of categories matter too because too many colours may cause chaos and make the visualization unreadable. You also have to consider that the colour choices are safe if you want to print your visualizations. 

Useful ggplot packages for colours are: viridis, RColorBrewer and paletteer.

## Linguistic Database Repository

### Database Types

Summarise the main types of linguistic databases and describe the key features that distinguish them from one another.

### Choosing Database for your Research

Choosing the right database depends on what aspect of language you want to investigate.

For **typological research**, [WALS](https://wals.info) (World Atlas of Language Structures) is the most widely used database. It contains over 200 linguistic features like word order, case marking, and phoneme inventories, each displayed on an interactive world map across thousands of languages. [AUTOTYP](https://www.autotyp.uzh.ch) is a good alternative that focuses more on how grammatical categories interact with each other, for example how case marking, agreement, and clause linkage work together. It provides more fine-grained morphosyntactic data than WALS.

For **historical and comparative linguistics**, [Glottolog](https://glottolog.org) is the main reference. It covers nearly all known languages with their genealogical classification, geographic location, and bibliographic references. It doesn't contain grammatical features like WALS, but it's essential when you need to know which language family a language belongs to or find published descriptions of a language.

For **corpus-based research**, [BNC](http://www.natcorp.ox.ac.uk) (British National Corpus) and [COCA](https://www.english-corpora.org/coca/) (Corpus of Contemporary American English) are commonly used for studying things like word frequency, collocations, and usage patterns in English. For research on language acquisition, [CHILDES](https://childes.talkbank.org) contains transcribed conversations between children and caregivers in many languages and is the standard resource in the field.

For **phonetics and phonology**, [PHOIBLE](https://phoible.org) collects phonological inventories from across the world's languages, documenting which consonants, vowels, and tones each language uses. It's useful for cross-linguistic comparisons of sound systems.

For **endangered and under-documented languages**, [ELAR](https://www.elararchive.org) (Endangered Languages Archive) and [PARADISEC](https://www.paradisec.org.au) store audio and video recordings, transcriptions, and other field data from languages that have very limited documentation.

In many cases, combining databases gives you a more complete picture. For example, a typological study could draw structural data from WALS and genealogical information from Glottolog to investigate whether a cross-linguistic pattern is driven by shared ancestry or independent development.

## Handling messy data with *tidyverse*

### *Tidyverse* umbrella

The [tidyverse](https://tidyverse.org/) consists of a collection of R packages. New packages get added frequently.

- **Tidyr** is used to clean data and helps to turn "messy" data into a tidy format. 
- **dplyr** is used to manipulate and join data and provides functions to filter rows, select columns and reorder rows.
- **tibble** provides re-imagining of the classic data frame and makes working with data structures in R cleaner and keeps the console output neat.
- **ggplot2** is used to plot your data and to visualise it. You can visualise your data layer by layer. 
- **readr** is designed to import data into R and provides a fast way to read rectangular data like CSV, TSV or log files.
- **stringr** is used for string manipulation.
- **forcats** is used for factors in R and helps to reorder, rename or change the levels of a factor.
- **lubridate** makes it easier to work with dates and times and simplifies parsing, manipulating and doing arithmetic with time-stamps.
- **purrr** enhances R's functional programming toolkit and allows you to apply functions to data.

### *Ggplot2* cheat sheet

*ggplot()* initialises a plot object

Different type of plots:
    *geom_point()* creates a scatter plot
    *geom_line()* creates a line plot
    *geom_bar()* creates a bar plot
    *geom_col()* creates a column plot
    *geom_histogram()* creates a histogram
    *geom_boxplot()* creates a box plot
    *geom_violin()* creates a violin plot
    *geom_density()* creates a density plot
    *geom_smooth()* adds a smoothed line to the plot

Core aesthetics:
    *aes(x, y, color, fill, size, shape, alpha)*
    where x and y define the horizontal and vertical axes, color and fill control the color, size controls the size of points or line, shape controls the point symbol, and alpha controls the transparency.

Further parameters are 
    - *linetype* to control the line style (dashed, dotted or solid)
    - *group* to specify how observations are grouped

You can also adjust the labels and titles using *labs(title = "Your Title", x = "X-axis Label", y = "Y-axis Label")* and *theme()*, where labs() takes care of titles and axis labels, and theme(), like theme_minimal(), theme_bw() and theme_classic(), allows you to customize the overall appearance of the plot, including text size, font, background, and grid lines.
You can flip the axes using *coord_flip()*


## Compiling an R Markdown document

### Markdown Output Formats

The main output formats are HTML, PDF and Microsoft Word (docx).
#### HTML Markdown Format
HTML is usefull when publishing directly on a website, blogs and other online documentation because HTML is the standard language for websites.
#### PDF Markdown Format
PDF is usefull for a final report, papers, books and other finalised publications because it preserves its formatting over all devices.
#### DOCX Markdown Format
DOCX is usefull for collaborative work as well as files that need further editing.

### Markdown Text Formatting

To create headings in a markdown file, precede the text in question with the `#` symbol, followed by a space. The size of the heading can be changed by adding several `#` symbols. The more symbols precede the text line, the smaller the heading will appear, thus also being lower in the hierarchy. 

Text styles can be changed with different symbols. To write in bold, the text must be surrounded by two `*` or `_` symbols on either side (e.g. `**bold**`). Italics require only one `*` or `_` symbol on both sides of the text. Strikethrough text can be used by using either one or two `~` symbols on either side of the text. 

One can also indicate quotes in markdown by preceding the text with the `> symbol. This creates an indent with a line to the left to set apart the quote from the rest of the text. 

To quote code, surround the text in questions with backticks `. 


Lists can be created in two ways: Unordered lists use lines preceded by the `-`, `*`, or `+` symbols. Using any of these symbols will create the same bulletted list format. List can also be ordered by writing a number in front of the text on each line. 
To nest lists, type spaces in front of the text line that lies below the first list item. This can then be repeated for the items that lie underneath the first nested line. 


Links can also be provided in text by typing brackets `[]` around link text, followed by parentheses `()` around the URL. Here is an example: `[Linguistic Data Science Class Library](https://github.com/UZH-Linguistic-Data-Science-Class-2026/project-lib/)`


To display images in a markdown file, type ! followed by brackets containing the alt text. Finally, add parentheses around the link to the image. 


To display a given text as a footnote, it must be followed by brackets containing the `^` symbol with a number after it. It should look like this: `Text[^1].` 

### Markdown Citations

Explain how to create cross-references within a document, generate a bibliography, and properly add citations.

Cross-references can be used to link other sections within the same document. This is done using anchor links. For example, if you have a heading called like this: 

## Results 

you can link to it with: 

[Go to Results](#results)

Citations can be added using citation keys inside square brakcets. For example: 

Language diversity has been wiedely studied [@croft2003]. 

You can also include multiple citations at the same time. For example:

[@croft2003; @dixon2010]

To create a bibliography, connect a `.bib`file in the YAML header: 

bibliography: references.bib

The `.bib` file contains the information about your references. When the document is rendered, R Markdown automatically creates a Reference section with all cited sources. 



### Formatting Tables 

#Explain how to create tables and captions, and describe the main table formatting options available in R Markdown.

There are different options of creating tables in an R Markdown file.

#### 1. Using 'Pipes' for simple tables:

```{r}
#Table: Table 1: Names, ages and animals

#| Name | Age | Animal |
#|------|-----|------|
#| Mirjam | 21  | Duck |
#| Sally | 25  | Frog   |
#| Dorina | 22  | Raccoon  |
```

Table: Table 1: Names, ages and animals

| Name | Age | Animal |
|------|-----|------|
| Mirjam | 21  | Duck |
| Sally | 25  | Frog   |
| Dorina | 22  | Raccoon  |

To add a caption to your table, you just need to write your desired caption on top of the table with a preceeding "Table:".

#### 2. Using 'knitr::kable()' function:

```{r}
library(knitr)

data <- data.frame(
    Name = c("Mirjam", "Sally", "Dorina"),
    Age = c(21.2202, 25.1703, 22.2802),
    Animal = c("Duck", "Frog", "Raccoon")
)

kable(data, caption = "Table 2: Names, ages and animals")
```
To add a caption, just define your desired caption in the "caption" variable.

#### 2.1 Formatting using 'knitr::kable()':
Usign 'knitr' you can format your data easily.
- Alignment: Aligning the columns left, center or right
```{r}
kable(data, align = c("l", "c", "r"))
```
- Number formatting: How many decimals should be displayed
```{r}
kable(data, digits = 2)
```

#### 3. Using 'table()' function to count frequencies:

```{r}
Animals <- c("Duck", "Duck", "Frog", "Raccoon", "Frog")

#table(animals)  <--- This works and produces a table, with that you just won't be able to add a caption
knitr::kable(table(Animals), caption = "Table 3: Frequency of animals")
```
To add a caption, you need to wrap the 'table()' function into the kable() function and define your 'caption' variable.
Using 'kable()' also makes the table a lot prettier than just the plain 'table()' table.

#### Further literature on RMD tables:
I found this interesting paper from the R-Project organisation themselves. It's a detailed paper on how to create different and more complex tables than just these three rather simple ones introduced.
If you're interested, go check it out: [Tables in R PDF URL](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DescTools/vignettes/TablesInR.pdf)
